question: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C#?
answer: A class is a reference type (you share the original). A struct is a value type (you make a copy).
whyAsked: Interviewers want to see if you understand how memory works. Passing a massive struct by accident can cause huge performance issues because you are copying it every time.
mistakes: Saying structs cannot have methods (they absolutely can).
Forgetting that if you change a struct variable, the original doesn't change because it's a copy.
interviewPitch: The main difference is how they are stored and passed around. A **class** is a reference type stored on the heap. If you pass a class to a method, you are passing a reference to the original object. A **struct** is a value type stored on the stack. If you pass a struct, you are passing a complete copy of the data. Because of this, I only use structs for very small, simple data (like a Point with X and Y) where copying is cheap. For everything else, I use a class.
explanation:
**🚗 The Car Analogy:**
• **Class (Reference Type):** You give your friend the keys to your car. If your friend paints the car red, **your car is now red**. You both share the exact same car.
• **Struct (Value Type):** You give your friend a 3D-printed exact replica of your car. If your friend paints their replica red, **your real car stays the original color**. They just modified their copy.

**When to use what:**
• **Use a Class (99% of the time):** For almost everything. Services, users, large objects.
• **Use a Struct (1% of the time):** Only for tiny pieces of data under 16 bytes (like coordinates, colors, or mathematical vectors).
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Class Assignment (Reference)
    A1[Variable A] --> O1((Object on Heap))
    B1[Variable B] --> O1
    end
    subgraph Struct Assignment (Copy)
    A2[Variable A] --> V1[Value 1 on Stack]
    B2[Variable B] --> V2[Value 2 on Stack]
    end

question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
answer: An abstract class is a half-finished blueprint that can have real code inside it. An interface is just a contract that forces a class to have certain methods, but has no actual code.
whyAsked: This is a fundamental object-oriented programming question. It shows if you know how to architect an application properly.
mistakes: Forgetting that a class can implement MULTIPLE interfaces, but can only inherit from ONE abstract class.
Saying interfaces can have state/fields (they cannot).
interviewPitch: An **abstract class** provides a shared base with partial implementation—it can have fields, constructors, and real method logic. You use it when related classes share common behavior. An **interface** is a pure contract with no state. The key advantage is that a class can implement **multiple interfaces**, but it can only inherit from **one abstract class**. I use abstract classes when there is shared logic, and interfaces when I need to define a capability that unrelated classes share.
explanation:
**📄 The Blueprint vs The Driver's License Analogy:**
• **Abstract Class (The Blueprint):** Imagine a blueprint for a `Vehicle`. It has an engine already built in (real code), but the `Drive()` method is left blank because a car drives differently than a boat. You can only use one blueprint to build your vehicle.
• **Interface (The License):** Imagine an `IDriveable` license. It doesn't give you a car, it just proves you know *how* to drive. A person can hold many licenses (`IDriveable`, `IFlyable`, `ISwimmable`).

**The Big Rule:**
Because C# only allows you to inherit from ONE class, you should always prefer Interfaces unless you absolutely need to share actual code (like fields or helper methods).
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A[Abstract Class: Vehicle
    - Has Engine
    - Drive()] --> C1[Car]
    A --> C2[Boat]
    
    I1[Interface: IDriveable] --> P[Person]
    I2[Interface: ISwimmable] --> P

question: How does Garbage Collection (GC) work in .NET?
answer: The Garbage Collector automatically frees up memory your app is no longer using. It sorts memory into 3 'Generations' to clean up short-lived objects quickly and leave long-lived objects alone.
whyAsked: Memory leaks can bring down entire servers. Interviewers want to know you understand how memory is managed so you don't write code that crashes the app under heavy load.
mistakes: Thinking C# never leaks memory (It does! Static variables and un-unsubscribed events will stay in memory forever).
Calling `GC.Collect()` manually. Never do this in production, it freezes the app.
interviewPitch: The .NET Garbage Collector is an automatic memory manager that works on a generational model. It divides the heap into three generations: Gen 0, Gen 1, and Gen 2. New objects go into Gen 0, which is collected very frequently because most objects are short-lived. If an object survives, it gets promoted to Gen 1, and eventually Gen 2. Gen 2 collections are expensive and rare. During a collection, the GC builds a graph of all reachable objects from the application roots, and any object not connected to the graph is deleted to free up memory.
explanation:
**🕺 The Nightclub Bouncer Analogy:**
Imagine the Garbage Collector is a bouncer at a nightclub, and the memory generations are different rooms.
• **Gen 0 (The Dance Floor):** People come and go very quickly. The bouncer checks this room constantly and clears out anyone who stopped dancing. (Fastest).
• **Gen 1 (The VIP Lounge):** If you survive the dance floor, you move here. The bouncer checks this room less often.
• **Gen 2 (The Staff Room):** If you survive the VIP lounge, you move here. You are probably staying all night. The bouncer almost never checks this room because it takes too long. (Slowest).

**How does it know what is garbage?**
It traces everything back to the 'roots' (like active variables currently in use). If an object is floating in memory but no active variable is pointing to it, the GC considers it garbage and deletes it.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    A[New Object Created] --> B[Gen 0]
    B -->|Survives GC| C[Gen 1]
    C -->|Survives GC| D[Gen 2]
    B -->|Is Garbage| E[Deleted immediately]
    C -->|Is Garbage| E

question: What is the difference between IEnumerable and IQueryable?
answer: IEnumerable filters data in your app's memory. IQueryable translates your C# code into SQL and filters the data directly on the database server.
whyAsked: This is a massive performance trap. Using IEnumerable instead of IQueryable on a database query will download the entire database into your app's RAM.
mistakes: Using .ToList() before filtering. `.ToList()` instantly turns an IQueryable into an IEnumerable, ruining the performance.
interviewPitch: The difference is where the filtering happens. **IEnumerable** works with in-memory collections. If you use it on a database table, it will pull every single row into your application's RAM, and then filter it. **IQueryable** inherits from IEnumerable, but it builds an Expression Tree. Providers like Entity Framework translate this tree directly into a SQL query. This means the filtering happens on the database server, and only the results are sent over the network. Always use IQueryable when querying a database.
explanation:
**🛒 The Grocery Store Analogy:**
You want to buy a carton of milk.
• **IEnumerable:** You buy *every single item* in the entire grocery store, bring it all to your house, put the milk in your fridge, and throw the rest in the trash. (Terrible performance).
• **IQueryable:** You hand the store clerk a note that says "Get me milk". The clerk goes into the store, gets ONLY the milk, and hands it to you. (Extremely efficient).

**The Golden Rule:**
Never call `.ToList()`, `.ToArray()`, or `.AsEnumerable()` until you are completely done filtering your data with `.Where()`.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant DB
    
    Note over App, DB: ❌ IEnumerable (Downloads everything!)
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM Users
    DB-->>App: Returns 1,000,000 Users
    App->>App: Filters for "Admins" in RAM
    
    Note over App, DB: ✅ IQueryable (Filters in Database!)
    App->>DB: SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Role='Admin'
    DB-->>App: Returns 5 Admins

question: Explain how async and await work under the hood in C#.
answer: Async/await frees up your application's threads while waiting for things like network requests or database queries. It does NOT create new threads; it simply lets the current thread go do other work until the result is ready.
whyAsked: Many developers think `async` magically makes code faster or runs it in parallel. Interviewers want to know you actually understand thread pooling and non-blocking I/O.
mistakes: Saying 'async creates a new thread'. It absolutely does not.
Using `.Result` or `.Wait()` on an async method. This causes the app to freeze (a deadlock).
interviewPitch: When the compiler sees `async/await`, it transforms the method into a **state machine**. When execution hits an `await` on an incomplete task (like a database query), the state machine saves where it paused and **returns the thread to the Thread Pool**. That thread is now free to handle other users' requests. When the database query finishes, the operating system signals the app, and a free thread from the pool picks up the state machine and continues the rest of the method. The key concept is: **no thread is ever blocked** waiting for I/O.
explanation:
**🍕 The Pizza Oven Analogy:**
• **Synchronous (Blocking):** You put a pizza in the oven. You stand there staring at the oven for 20 minutes doing absolutely nothing until it's done. You are "blocked".
• **Asynchronous (Async/Await):** You put the pizza in the oven and set a timer (`await`). You walk away to wash dishes or watch TV. When the timer beeps, you go back to the oven. You got a lot of other work done while waiting!

**Does it make my code faster?**
No! A 2-second database query still takes 2 seconds. What it does is make your *server* handle more traffic. Instead of 100 threads standing around staring at the database, those 100 threads are free to serve other web requests.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Thread
    participant DB
    
    Note over Thread, DB: ❌ Synchronous (Thread is trapped!)
    Thread->>DB: Send Query
    Note over Thread: Thread sits here asleep for 2 seconds
    DB-->>Thread: Results
    
    Note over Thread, DB: ✅ Asynchronous (Thread is free!)
    Thread->>DB: Send Query (await)
    Note over Thread: Thread leaves to go serve other users!
    DB-->>Thread: Results are ready!
    Note over Thread: Thread comes back and resumes code.

question: What is the difference between the 'ref' and 'out' keywords?
answer: Both let a method modify the original variable you passed in. The difference is: 'ref' requires the variable to have a value BEFORE you pass it. 'out' forces the method to assign a value INSIDE the method.
whyAsked: This checks your understanding of passing by reference. `out` is incredibly common in C# because of the `TryParse` pattern.
mistakes: Forgetting to assign a value to an `out` parameter before the method finishes (the compiler will yell at you).
interviewPitch: Both `ref` and `out` pass arguments by reference instead of by value, meaning the method works with the original variable. The main difference is the initialization rule. `ref` requires the variable to be initialized **before** you pass it in, and the method can choose to read it or modify it. `out` does not require prior initialization, but the method **must** assign a value to it before returning. I use `out` all the time for methods that need to return multiple values, like the `int.TryParse` pattern.
explanation:
**🎁 The Magic Box Analogy:**
• **`ref` (The Transformation Box):** You put a toy car in a box and hand it to a magician. The magician changes it into a toy boat and gives it back. You *must* put something in the box first.
• **`out` (The Empty Box):** You hand the magician a completely empty box. The magician is forced by law to put a toy inside before handing it back to you. You *do not* need to put anything in the box first.

**When to use `out`:**
In C#, methods can only `return` one thing. If you want to return a `bool` AND an `int`, you can return the `bool` normally, and use an `out` parameter to send the `int` back.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph ref (Requires Value)
    A1[int x = 5] --> M1((Method))
    M1 -->|Reads 5, Changes to 10| R1[x is now 10]
    end
    subgraph out (Requires Assignment)
    A2[int y] --> M2((Method))
    M2 -->|MUST assign y = 99| R2[y is now 99]
    end

question: What is the difference between .NET Framework, .NET Core, and .NET 5/6/7/8?
answer: .NET Framework is the old, Windows-only version. .NET Core was the modern, cross-platform rewrite. Starting with .NET 5, they combined everything into one single platform just called '.NET'.
whyAsked: This is almost always the very first question in a .NET interview. It proves you understand the history of the ecosystem and aren't confusing ancient technology with modern technology.
mistakes: Saying .NET Core is a 'lighter version' of .NET Framework (It's a complete rewrite).
Confusing .NET Standard with .NET 5 or .NET 8.
interviewPitch: .NET Framework is the original, Windows-only platform that came out in 2002. It's now basically in maintenance mode. .NET Core was built from the ground up in 2016 to be cross-platform, open-source, and extremely fast. Then, in 2020, Microsoft unified the ecosystem with .NET 5. They dropped the word 'Core', so .NET 6, 7, and 8 are the direct modern successors to .NET Core. I always target the latest Long Term Support (LTS) version, like .NET 8, for new projects because of the massive performance benefits and cross-platform support.
explanation:
**🚗 The Car Analogy:**
• **.NET Framework:** A classic, heavy gas-powered truck. It only drives on one specific type of road (Windows). It's reliable, but old and no longer getting new engine upgrades.
• **.NET Core:** A completely redesigned electric sports car. It's incredibly fast, lightweight, and can drive on any road (Windows, Mac, Linux).
• **.NET 8:** The newest model of that electric sports car. They stopped putting 'Core' in the name because it's now the only car the factory makes.

**Why did we switch to Core?**
Before Core, if you wrote a .NET backend, you *had* to host it on an expensive Windows Server. Now, you can host it on cheap Linux servers or Docker containers, saving companies thousands of dollars.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    F[.NET Framework (2002)] -->|Windows Only| M[Maintenance Mode]
    C[.NET Core 1-3 (2016)] -->|Cross Platform| N5[.NET 5 (Unified)]
    N5 --> N6[.NET 6 LTS]
    N6 --> N7[.NET 7]
    N7 --> N8[.NET 8 LTS (Modern!)]

question: What is Boxing and Unboxing in C#?
answer: Boxing is taking a simple, fast Value Type (like an int) and wrapping it inside a heavy Reference Type (an object). Unboxing is ripping it back out. Both are slow and should be avoided.
whyAsked: This is a hidden performance killer. Interviewers want to know you won't accidentally slow down the application by doing this inside a big loop.
mistakes: Not realizing that passing an `int` to a method that asks for an `object` secretly causes boxing.
Using old collections like `ArrayList` instead of `List<int>`.
interviewPitch: Boxing is the process of converting a Value Type (which lives on the stack) into an `object` (which lives on the heap). Unboxing is casting it back from an object to a Value Type. Both of these operations are computationally expensive because they require memory allocation on the heap and create extra work for the Garbage Collector. Today, we almost entirely avoid boxing by using Generics (like `List<int>` instead of the old `ArrayList`).
explanation:
**📦 The Locked Box Analogy:**
Imagine you have a piece of paper with the number 42 written on it (A Value Type).
• **Boxing:** You buy a heavy, metal safe (an Object), put the paper inside, lock it, and hire a moving company to carry the safe to a warehouse (the Heap).
• **Unboxing:** You go to the warehouse, hire a locksmith to open the safe, take the paper out, and carry it back home.

If you do this 1,000,000 times in a loop, your app will freeze. It's a massive waste of time and energy when you could have just kept the piece of paper in your pocket!
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Stack
    participant Heap
    
    Note over Stack, Heap: 📦 Boxing (Slow Allocation)
    Stack->>Heap: int x = 5 (Wrap in Object)
    Note over Heap: Creates Garbage!
    
    Note over Stack, Heap: 📤 Unboxing (Slow Cast)
    Heap->>Stack: int y = (int)obj

question: What are Delegates and Events in C#?
answer: A Delegate is a variable that holds a method instead of data. An Event is a special wrapper around a delegate that acts like a broadcast system—when something happens, it notifies everyone who subscribed.
whyAsked: This is how C# handles all UI clicks, background task completions, and system notifications. You can't write advanced C# without understanding them.
mistakes: Confusing them: A delegate is the underlying plumbing. An event is just a safe wrapper over the plumbing so outside classes can't accidentally break it.
Forgetting to unsubscribe from events (which causes massive memory leaks!).
interviewPitch: A **delegate** is a type-safe function pointer. Instead of holding data like an integer, it holds a reference to a method. You can pass methods around as variables. An **event** is a specialized, restricted delegate based on the Publisher-Subscriber pattern. The restriction is that outside classes can only subscribe (`+=`) or unsubscribe (`-=`) to the event; they cannot invoke it or clear it. Only the class that owns the event can trigger it. Today, we mostly use the built-in `Action` and `Func` delegates instead of creating custom ones.
explanation:
**📺 The YouTube Analogy:**
• **Delegate:** Think of a delegate as a piece of paper with a phone number on it. If you call the number, it plays a video. You can give this paper to anyone.
• **Event:** Think of an Event as a YouTube Channel. 
    - **Subscribing (`+=`):** Viewers click "Subscribe".
    - **Publishing (`Invoke()`):** The YouTuber uploads a video, and YouTube automatically notifies every single person who subscribed. 
    - **The Restriction:** Viewers cannot upload videos to the channel, and viewers cannot delete other subscribers. Only the YouTuber has that power. That is why Events are safer than raw Delegates.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    P[Publisher Class
    Triggers Event] -->|Notifies| S1[Subscriber A (Sends Email)]
    P -->|Notifies| S2[Subscriber B (Writes to Log)]
    P -.->|Cannot Notify| S3[Did not subscribe]

question: What are Generics in C#? Why use them?
answer: Generics let you write a single class or method that works with ANY data type, while still being type-safe. It prevents code duplication and stops the deadly 'Boxing' performance issue.
whyAsked: Generics are the foundation of modern C#. Everything from `List<T>` to `Task<T>` uses them. If you don't understand `<T>`, you can't read C# code.
mistakes: Thinking you have to use the letter `T`. (You can name it `<TEntity>` or `<TModel>`, `T` is just a convention for 'Type').
Not knowing about Generic Constraints (`where T : class`), which let you lock down what types are allowed.
interviewPitch: Generics allow us to design classes and methods that defer the specification of one or more types until the class or method is actually declared. We use the `<T>` syntax for this. The two massive benefits are **code reusability** (we don't have to write a separate `IntList` and `StringList` class) and **type safety** (the compiler guarantees you can't accidentally put a string into a `List<int>`). Furthermore, Generics completely eliminate the performance penalty of Boxing that we used to have with old `object`-based collections.
explanation:
**🥡 The Tupperware Analogy:**
Imagine you want to store leftover food.
• **The Old Way (No Generics):** You have a generic `ObjectBox`. You put a piece of pizza in it. Later, someone reaches in blindly, thinks it's cake, takes a bite, and ruins their dessert. (Not type-safe!).
• **The Hard Way:** You build a specific `PizzaBox`, a specific `CakeBox`, and a specific `SaladBox`. (Massive code duplication, waste of time).
• **The Generic Way (`Box<T>`):** You buy a magical Tupperware container. When you buy it, you label it `Box<Pizza>`. From that moment on, the container will ONLY accept Pizza. If someone tries to put Cake in it, the container physically rejects it (Compiler error!).
diagram:
flowchart TD
    G[Generic List<T>] -->|T becomes int| L1[List<int>]
    G -->|T becomes string| L2[List<string>]
    G -->|T becomes User| L3[List<User>]
    
    L1 -.->|Type Safe!| E[No Boxing! No Casting!]

question: What is LINQ? Give a real example.
answer: LINQ (Language Integrated Query) is a set of features in C# that lets you search, filter, and sort lists of data using simple, readable commands instead of writing massive `foreach` loops.
whyAsked: Nobody writes manual 'for' loops to search arrays anymore. LINQ is used in literally every single C# codebase in the world.
mistakes: Writing a 10-line `foreach` loop with `if` statements instead of a 1-line `.Where().Select()`.
Forgetting that LINQ doesn't actually run until you call `.ToList()` or `.FirstOrDefault()` (Deferred Execution).
interviewPitch: LINQ stands for Language Integrated Query. It provides a unified, readable syntax to query any data source—whether it's an in-memory List, an XML document, or a SQL database via Entity Framework. It replaces verbose `foreach` loops with declarative, functional-style methods like `.Where()`, `.Select()`, and `.OrderBy()`. The most important concept in LINQ is **Deferred Execution**: a LINQ query is just a set of instructions. The query does not actually execute and process the data until you force it to materialize by calling a method like `.ToList()` or iterating over it.
explanation:
**🍔 The Drive-Thru Analogy:**
Imagine you have a huge menu of 100 items.
• **The `foreach` loop way:** You go into the kitchen, look at all 100 items one by one, and if an item is a burger, you put it on a tray. Then you sort the tray by price.
• **The LINQ way:** You go to the drive-thru window and say: *"Give me all the Burgers, ordered by price."* (`menu.Where(m => m.IsBurger).OrderBy(m => m.Price)`). LINQ handles all the kitchen work for you, instantly.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    Data[Raw Data List] --> W[.Where(x > 10)]
    W --> O[.OrderBy(x)]
    O --> S[.Select(Name)]
    S -->|Wait until .ToList()| R[Final Filtered List]

question: What are Records in C# and when do you use them?
answer: A record is a special kind of class designed for data that should NEVER change (immutable). It automatically writes equality checks for you, so two records with the same data are considered completely equal.
whyAsked: Records were introduced in C# 9 and are extremely popular in modern APIs and Microservices. Interviewers want to see if you are keeping up with modern C# features.
mistakes: Using a Record for something that changes often, like a `ShoppingCart`.
Not knowing the `with` keyword, which lets you easily make a copy of a record with slight changes.
interviewPitch: A `record` is a reference type (like a class) introduced in C# 9 that provides built-in functionality for encapsulating data. The two main features are **Immutability** (they are usually read-only) and **Value-based Equality**. With normal classes, `obj1 == obj2` only returns true if they are the exact same object in memory. With records, `rec1 == rec2` returns true if their *properties* hold the exact same data. I use records almost exclusively for DTOs (Data Transfer Objects), API responses, and configuration settings because they are lightweight and safe from accidental modification.
explanation:
**🧾 The Store Receipt Analogy:**
• **Class (The Whiteboard):** You write a grocery list on a whiteboard. Anyone can walk by, erase "Apples", and write "Candy". It mutates (changes).
• **Record (The Printed Receipt):** The cashier hands you a printed paper receipt. It is permanent. If you want a receipt that says "Candy", you can't erase the ink—you have to return the item and print a brand new receipt. 

**Why is this good?**
In complex apps, if data can't change, it can't be broken by accident by another part of the code. It makes debugging 10x easier.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Class Equality (Checks Memory Address)
    C1[new Class(X=5)] 
    C2[new Class(X=5)]
    C1 -.->|Not Equal!| C2
    end
    subgraph Record Equality (Checks Actual Data)
    R1[new Record(X=5)]
    R2[new Record(X=5)]
    R1 -->|Is Equal!| R2
    end

question: What is the difference between String and StringBuilder?
answer: A normal String is immutable—every time you change it, it destroys the old string and creates a brand new one in memory. StringBuilder is mutable—it acts like a notebook where you can keep adding text without wasting memory.
whyAsked: Doing `text += "a"` inside a massive loop will literally crash an application due to Out Of Memory exceptions. This tests if you know how to build large strings safely.
mistakes: Using StringBuilder for just 2 or 3 strings. (Just use normal string interpolation `$"{a} {b}"`, StringBuilder is only for loops).
Not knowing that Strings are immutable in C#.
interviewPitch: In C#, strings are **immutable**. This means once a string is created in memory, it cannot be modified. If you concatenate strings using the `+=` operator in a loop, it allocates a brand new string on the heap every single iteration, creating massive Garbage Collection pressure. **StringBuilder** solves this. It allocates a buffer of memory and allows you to continuously append characters to that same buffer without creating new objects. I always use `StringBuilder` when I am generating large text documents, HTML, or looping more than a dozen times.
explanation:
**📝 The Tape vs The Notebook Analogy:**
• **String (The Tape Way):** You have a piece of paper that says "A". You want it to say "AB". You are not allowed to use a pencil. Instead, you have to throw the paper in the trash, buy a brand new piece of paper, and write "AB". If you do this 10,000 times, your trashcan (the Garbage Collector) overflows.
• **StringBuilder (The Notebook Way):** You buy a notebook. You write "A". Then you just write "B" right next to it. No trash, no wasted paper. Fast and efficient.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Code
    participant Memory
    
    Note over Code, Memory: ❌ String Concatenation
    Code->>Memory: Create "A"
    Code->>Memory: Create "AB" (Throw away "A")
    Code->>Memory: Create "ABC" (Throw away "AB")
    Note over Memory: Memory is full of garbage!
    
    Note over Code, Memory: ✅ StringBuilder
    Code->>Memory: Create Buffer [        ]
    Code->>Memory: Add "A" -> [A       ]
    Code->>Memory: Add "B" -> [AB      ]
    Note over Memory: Clean and Fast!

question: What are the different types of Collections in C# (List, Dictionary, HashSet)?
answer: A List is an ordered array (use for normal lists). A Dictionary stores Key/Value pairs for instant lookups. A HashSet stores unique items for instant 'Contains' checks.
whyAsked: If you use a `List` to search through 1 million items, it takes forever. If you use a `HashSet`, it is instant. Interviewers want to know you pick the right tool for the job.
mistakes: Using `.Contains()` on a giant `List` instead of a `HashSet`. (O(N) vs O(1) performance).
Using a `Dictionary` when you don't actually need the Key, just the uniqueness.
interviewPitch: Choosing the right collection dictates the performance (Big O notation) of your app. **List<T>** is an ordered, dynamically sized array. It is great for iterating, but searching (`.Contains()`) is O(N) slow. **Dictionary<TKey, TValue>** is a hash table. It stores key-value pairs and provides incredibly fast O(1) lookups by key. **HashSet<T>** is like a Dictionary without values—it just stores unique keys. It is the absolute best choice when you need to quickly check if an item exists or remove duplicates.
explanation:
**🏢 The Real World Analogies:**
• **`List<T>` (The DMV Line):** Everyone stands in a specific order. If you want to find "Bob", you have to walk down the entire line checking every single person's face. Slow to search, but keeps everyone in perfect order.
• **`Dictionary<K, V>` (The Phonebook):** You want Alice's phone number. You don't read page 1, page 2, page 3. You instantly flip to 'A' and find her. Extremely fast lookup via a Key.
• **`HashSet<T>` (The VIP Bouncer):** The bouncer has a list of VIP names. When John walks up, the bouncer instantly knows if John is on the list or not. It prevents duplicates (you can't be on the VIP list twice).
diagram:
flowchart LR
    subgraph List (Order Matters)
    L1[1. Apple] --> L2[2. Banana] --> L3[3. Cherry]
    end
    subgraph Dictionary (Key/Value Fast Lookup)
    D1[Key: 101] -.-> V1[Value: Alice]
    D2[Key: 102] -.-> V2[Value: Bob]
    end
    subgraph HashSet (Unique Fast Lookup)
    H1((Apple)) --- H2((Banana))
    H1 --- H3((Cherry))
    end

question: What is Dependency Injection (DI)? Explain with a C# example.
answer: DI is a design pattern where you pass required objects (dependencies) into a class from the outside, instead of the class creating them itself using the `new` keyword.
whyAsked: Every modern .NET application is built on top of Dependency Injection. If you don't understand DI, you won't understand how ASP.NET Core controllers work.
mistakes: Using `new Database()` inside a class constructor. (This makes the class impossible to unit test).
Not knowing the difference between Singleton, Scoped, and Transient lifetimes.
interviewPitch: Dependency Injection is a technique to achieve Inversion of Control. Instead of a class instantiating its dependencies using the `new` keyword (which tightly couples them), the dependencies are provided to the class from the outside, usually via constructor injection. This makes the code **loosely coupled** and **highly testable**, because we can easily pass in a "Mock" database during unit testing. .NET Core has a built-in DI container where we register our services as Transient, Scoped, or Singleton.
explanation:
**🚚 The Grocery Delivery Analogy:**
Imagine you are a Chef (A Class) who needs Tomatoes (A Dependency) to cook.
• **The BAD Way (No DI):** You leave the kitchen, drive to the farm, plant a tomato seed, grow it, harvest it, and drive back. (`new Tomato()`). You are doing too much work, and if the farm closes, you can't cook.
• **The GOOD Way (Dependency Injection):** You stand in the kitchen. Someone knocks on the door and hands you fresh Tomatoes. You don't care where they came from or how they grew. You just take them and cook! 

**How we do it in C#:**
We write our classes to ask for things in their `Constructor`. Then, the .NET framework automatically delivers those things when the app runs.
